questions.q: A transfer debits one account and credits another in one transaction. Which ACID property ensures neither change applies without the other?
options: Isolation, which orders the two writes so readers never interleave them
Atomicity, which commits or rolls back the pair as a single unit
Durability, which persists both changes to disk before acknowledging
Consistency, which validates the account balances after each write

questions.q: Which workload most clearly favors a relational database over a key-value store?
options: Ad-hoc reports joining orders, customers, and inventory tables
Looking up session payloads by their unique session token
Caching rendered page fragments keyed by their URL
Storing device telemetry appended at very high rates

questions.q: In an eventually consistent store, what does the system actually promise about replicas?
options: Each replica acknowledges every write before any read gets served
Reads always reflect the most recent successful write
Given no new writes, all replicas converge to the same value
Conflicting writes are impossible because replicas take turns

questions.q: Which NoSQL family is purpose-built for traversing relationships like 'friends of friends'?
options: Wide-column stores, which group related columns into families
Document stores, which nest related records inside a single document
Key-value stores, which link records through composite keys
Graph databases, storing nodes and edges as first-class data

questions.q: Why do self-contained documents make horizontal write scaling simpler than normalized relational rows?
options: A document shards as one unit, avoiding cross-node joins on reads and writes
JSON serializes faster than the relational wire protocols used by SQL databases
Documents compress better, so each shard holds proportionally more data
Document stores buffer writes in memory while relational engines cannot

questions.q: What does 'schema-on-write' mean in practice for a relational table?
options: The schema is versioned automatically so old rows keep their original column layout forever
Readers must supply a schema to interpret the raw stored bytes
Inserts violating declared column types or constraints are rejected immediately
The schema can only change by rebuilding the table from scratch

questions.q: A cart service needs microsecond lookups by session id and no other query patterns. Best fit?
options: A fully normalized relational schema with the cart split across five joined tables
An in-memory key-value store mapping session id to the cart blob
A document store with secondary indexes on every cart field
A graph database linking session nodes to product nodes

questions.q: To stay writable during network partitions, Dynamo-style stores historically relaxed which guarantee?
options: Durability, acknowledging writes before replicating them anywhere
Client authentication during the partition window
Per-key write atomicity on the accepting replica
Strong consistency, letting replicas briefly diverge and reconcile later

questions.q: An order flow must atomically update accounts, ledger, and audit tables. Why does a basic key-value store struggle?
options: Key-value stores cannot represent monetary values without floating point error
Each table would need its own separate cluster, tripling operational cost
It offers atomicity per key, but no transaction spanning arbitrary keys
Its eventual durability means committed writes may vanish after a crash

questions.q: Fields on your user profile change every sprint, and reads are by primary key. What does a document store buy you here?
options: New optional fields ship without a coordinated table migration
Old documents are rewritten automatically to match the newest shape
Reads become transactional across all documents in the collection
Field renames propagate to historical documents at query time

questions.q: An analytics job scans two columns across billions of rows. Why does columnar storage beat row storage here?
options: Columnar engines cache the entire table in RAM between queries
Row stores must lock each row as it is scanned, throttling reads
Columnar files skip the transaction log entirely, roughly halving total write amplification
Only the two needed columns are read, and similar values compress tightly

questions.q: Why do relational joins degrade sharply once tables are sharded across many machines?
options: The SQL standard removes join support once a table is partitioned
Matching rows can live on different nodes, forcing large cross-network shuffles
Sharding invalidates secondary indexes, so every join falls back to full table scans
Join buffers are pinned to one primary node and cannot grow larger

questions.q: Seconds after you update your bio, a friend still sees the old one. In an eventually consistent store, what most likely happened?
options: Their read hit a replica the write had not yet reached
The write failed a validation rule and was silently rolled back
A row-level lock made their read return the column's default value
Read-repair deleted the newer value while reconciling replicas

questions.q: When does denormalizing shared data into each document backfire the most?
options: When documents are usually read in their entirety by the application
When the collection is sharded across more than a handful of nodes
When reads outnumber writes by several orders of magnitude
When many documents copy a value that changes frequently

questions.q: A team with 5 GB of data and heavy reporting adopts a key-value store 'for scale'. Most likely outcome?
options: Single-key reads become slower than relational primary-key lookups were
Joins and aggregations get re-implemented, badly, in application code
The store's strict schema checks reject most of their existing records
Write throughput drops because all writes serialize on one global lock

questions.q: Which access pattern most justifies a graph database over SQL join tables?
options: Fetching a user's direct friends list each time their profile page renders
Counting the total number of edges in the network for a daily report
Variable-depth traversals such as shortest path between two members
Sorting all users by signup date with pagination

questions.q: A global app needs sub-50 ms reads everywhere; payments need strict ordering; minor feed staleness is fine. Sound architecture?
options: One strongly consistent global database serving every workload from a single region
Everything eventually consistent, reconciling payment order in a nightly batch
Per-region relational primaries with clients writing to whichever is nearest
Geo-replicated eventual store for feeds, payments routed to one strongly consistent service

questions.q: Which statement best captures transactions in modern NoSQL systems?
options: Multi-document transactions remain impossible because BASE semantics forbid atomic commits entirely
Several offer multi-document ACID transactions, at a real throughput and latency cost
Transactions are now free because they run entirely on the client
Only graph databases gained transactions, since edges require them

questions.q: Postgres handles 5k writes/s at 60% CPU; load doubles yearly. Strongest argument to defer a Cassandra migration now?
options: Vertical headroom plus read replicas likely covers years, at far lower risk than migrating
Cassandra clusters cannot exceed the write rate of a tuned Postgres primary
Doubling load will halve CPU usage as caches warm over time
Postgres will scale writes automatically once partitioned tables are enabled

questions.q: Why are Cassandra-style data models designed starting from the queries rather than the entities?
options: CQL lacks a general WHERE clause, so most filtering must happen in the application layer
Entities cannot be represented because storage is a flat log of writes
Each query should hit one partition; cross-partition scans are slow and unbounded
The engine enforces third normal form, constraining table design
